📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).
  • It has been revealed that the team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style.
  • In a recent development, on the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

It has been revealed that the team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

In a recent development, on the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell.

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

Recent findings suggest that the expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell mentioned. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

Recent findings suggest that after the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram.

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

Recent findings suggest that the line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

In a recent development, on the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:.

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It has been revealed that it took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

Sources indicate that A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

Industry observers note that “The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram.

In a recent development, “You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”.

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”.

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell noted. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” stated Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell mentioned.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”.

According to recent reports, “Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”.

#102459. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (550 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails.
  • According to recent reports, before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Industry observers note that their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

According to recent reports, before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

According to recent reports, from there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Recent findings suggest that every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

The route. Photo: Pete Streufert.

Recent findings suggest that after 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” claims Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to Latest Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert.

A final paddling section on Newly introduced Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram.

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (273 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu.
  • Recent findings suggest that joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass.
  • According to recent reports, kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Recent findings suggest that joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

According to recent reports, kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

Recent findings suggest that the case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (631 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time.
  • Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening.
  • It has been revealed that everest West Ridge some days ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

It has been revealed that everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”.

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev.

Industry observers note that first, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

In a recent development, “Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev mentioned. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”.

Industry observers note that at the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that on their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” noted Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev stated:.

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Sources indicate that rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

It has been revealed that the route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

Sources indicate that the North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he remarked.

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

It has been revealed that the fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World.

Recent findings suggest that the winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

In a recent development, “I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”.

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more vital to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Photo: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World.

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World.

Industry observers note that in defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

In a recent development, these human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World.

Sources indicate that I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

According to recent reports, you can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously.
  • But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear.
  • The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

Recent findings suggest that they left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families remarked they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Industry observers note that kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

In a recent development, search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office mentioned in a Facebook post.

Industry observers note that multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office.

It has been revealed that rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities declared they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

Industry observers note that the Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

According to recent reports, from 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday.
  • Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

Recent findings suggest that the incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok remarked that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

According to recent reports, turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

Recent findings suggest that your own bank takes cash free on a personal account, so use its branch or one of its ATMs that accept deposits. If your bank is online-only, hand the cash to a partner store’s cashier, often for a few dollars, or deposit it at a local bank or credit union and transfer it to your online account.

Industry observers note that paying a few dollars to deposit your own cash adds up fast when tips or cash sales come in every week. Where you make the deposit decides whether you pay anything at all.

Your bank’s own ATMs also let you avoid ATM fees when you take cash out. If your credit union belongs to the Co-op Shared Branch network, other credit unions in it will take your deposit too, at more than 5,500 locations across the country.

According to recent reports, large deposits come with a federal rule. Your bank or credit union must report cash deposits of more than $10,000 in a day to the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, whatever the reason for them. It will ask for your ID and Social Security number to file that report. Depositing that much is allowed, but splitting it into smaller deposits to avoid the report is a crime called structuring, even when the cash came to you legally.

Many online banks and apps take cash at a store’s register, and the store may charge for it. With the Chime® app, cash deposits are free at Walgreens and Duane Reade, but other stores can charge up to $4.95 each time1. Capital One takes cash free at partner stores such as CVS and Walgreens for its checking and savings customers.

According to recent reports, the free workaround needs a second account. Picture a server who deposits her tips at her credit union’s ATM every week, then moves what she’s saving to an online savings account. At a store charging $4.95, those 52 deposits would cost her about $257 a year instead of nothing.

If cash comes in every week, open a no-fee checking account at a credit union or bank near work and link it to your online bank.

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Sources indicate that left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet.

In a recent development, the Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

  • Industry observers note that say you’re 15 and tutor two middle schoolers in math over video, each for one hour a week at $20 an hour.
  • Sources indicate that two sets of rules decide which online jobs you can take.
  • The second is federal child labor law, which applies when a business hires you as an employee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that say you’re 15 and tutor two middle schoolers in math over video, each for one hour a week at $20 an hour. Over a 36-week school year, that’s $40 a week and $1,440 in all.

Sources indicate that two sets of rules decide which online jobs you can take. The first is each site’s minimum age, and some sites let you work at 13 through an account a parent owns.

The second is federal child labor law, which applies when a business hires you as an employee. It sets 16 as the basic minimum age, and at 14 and 15 you can work only outside school hours, capped at 3 hours a school day and 18 hours a school week. Many states also require a work permit, and when state and federal rules both apply, the stricter one wins.

Sources indicate that the 18 jobs below are open to teens. In the first two lists, you find clients yourself among families and business owners you know, so no site sets an age. In the last two, the site takes teens on their own or through a parent’s account. Teens who’d rather work in person can look at part-time jobs for high school students instead.

Parents pick tutors they trust, so start with families from your school, your neighborhood, or a parent’s circle of friends. Charge about $20 an hour, like the tutor above, and raise it once families come back for more.

Recent findings suggest that start with owners you already know, like a parent’s friend who runs a salon, and agree on an hourly rate or a flat monthly fee in writing before you begin. A business that puts you on its payroll instead has to follow the federal limits above and your state’s child labor rules.

Each of these sites sets its own age rule, and each needs a parent on board before you list anything.

Keep a record of every payment you receive. IRS rules require you to file a return once your net earnings from self-employment reach $400 in a year, so the tutor above, at $1,440 with no costs, would file. The same goes for wages from a job that top the standard deduction for a single filer, the income the IRS doesn’t tax, even when your parents claim you as a dependent.

In a recent development, that same money can go into a custodial Roth IRA, a retirement account a parent opens and runs for you. The IRS sets no age limit for Roth IRA contributions, but you can’t put in more than you earned from work that year.

The FTC warns that real employers never charge you to get hired. So walk away from any job that asks you to pay first, whether for training, a starter kit, or equipment.

It has been revealed that explorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

According to recent reports, views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Industry observers note that piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

It has been revealed that the members work remotely, choosing from a Major List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Sources indicate that left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Massive List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

It has been revealed that the second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively fresh piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

In a recent development, interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

It has been revealed that finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the major list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

In a recent development, it is unclear whether the fresh additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

In a recent development, as for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

Industry observers note that the physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides.

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term strategy is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

#102443. Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1443 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1443 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny.
  • Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades.
  • So by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m a proponent of stealth wealth. It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny. The last thing you want to do is show off and put you and your family in danger.

Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades. If you keep living well below your means, which is required to retire early, your investments will eventually compound faster than you can spend.

So by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner. Whether they mean to or not.

In private, you can do whatever you want. But in public, staying low-key is better. Here are three simple steps to follow:.

Sources indicate that 1) Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.

Recent findings suggest that 2) Drive an old car. Driving a upcoming car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.

3) Stay quiet about your spending on social media. Don't post vacation photos or the nice things you buy. If a tree falls in Hawaii and nobody sees it on Instagram, did the vacation still happen? Yes, and it was more relaxing.

Do these three things and you’ll join the Stealth Wealth club, a group of operators who move in and out of the shadows unnoticed.

Once you’re in, you’ll realize there are far more members than you think. That realization is oddly bullish. A lot more people are doing better than the media or politicians would have you believe. They’re just not wearing it.

In 8th grade in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, I wanted two things: to be cool and to have girlfriends.

According to recent reports, my parents drove a 1976 Datsun with missing hubcaps. Getting dropped off in that car was social agony. So I had to find status elsewhere.

According to recent reports, at the time, there were two ways to increase your coolness as a teenager: be a good skateboarder or dress in designer clothes. I chose both.

I still remember forking over 160 ringgit, about $64 back then (roughly $150 today), for a used pair of Armani Exchange jeans. 30-inch waist, 31-inch cut length, bronze eagle triangle on the back pocket. That was an absurd amount of money for a 13-year-old to spend on pants. But all the cool rich kids had them, so I had to have them too.

It has been revealed that then came the equally expensive Doc Martens. Then a Guess shirt. Looking back, nearly all my work and allowance money went to clothes and shoes.

And you know what? I enjoyed it. It made me feel good, and I was part of the cool crowd with plenty of friends.

In a recent development, today, I couldn’t give two shitake mushrooms about designer labels. I want comfortable, practical clothes with zipper pockets so I don’t lose my wallet, phone, and keys. I cut my own hair to save time and money, and I usually cover it with a frayed baseball cap anyway.

So what happened between Armani jeans and black running pants?

I stopped needing respect from everyone.

I’m writing this post because of a clip from author Min Jin Lee explaining why some people with little money spend lavishly on material things. As personal finance enthusiasts, we shake our heads at such conspicuous spending. Don’t they want to eventually be financially free? We think to ourselves. But we’re missing something notable.

Her point: when you grow up in a poor community, respect matters enormously. It becomes a kind of currency. And when you don’t have much else, you tend to overvalue it. So you buy the nicer clothes, shoes, watches, and cars, hoping they command respect, even if it means carrying credit card debt.

This resonated with me as a minority who came to America for high school and faced various racist incidents. Racism is one of the deepest forms of disrespect because you're insulted just for being who you are. Respect, especially for elders, is a significant part of Asian culture. When people disrespect me online or in real life, it can be infuriating. In my younger years, I’d go after them to defend my honor.

In a recent development, when you think about it this way, materialism isn’t irrational. It’s a logical strategy for buying respect when you don’t have other ways to earn it. With this understanding, I'm going to try and be extra respectful to everybody I interact with from now on.

In a recent development, at 13, I spent a fortune on Armani jeans to earn respect from my skater friends and the girls I liked. When I started working in finance, I dressed to earn respect from my peers and bosses.

In a recent development, then I left finance in 2012. Overnight, the nice clothes went untouched. I no longer needed respect from anyone outside my home.

Funny enough, they're all still hanging in my closet 14 years later in pristine condition.

Recent findings suggest that today, insults from random folks feel more like pinches instead of body blows. The passive income is doing its job as a shield.

Recent findings suggest that as a dad now, the only people I want respect from are my wife and children. Having respect from my parents and sister would be nice too, but we don’t see each other day-to-day so it’s no major deal if not. As any parent and provider knows, taking care of a family is hard work.

As a result, on our family trip to Las Vegas, I confess that a part of me felt disrespected when my wife gave me a bothersome look when I asked her to take a few more profile photos of me at Redrocks.

In that moment, my brain immediately pulled up the receipts. I agreed to this $7,000 trip despite being in a liquidity crunch. I went to bed at 2 am and still woke up by 6 am to get everyone breakfast. What’s the big deal?

Yes, I realize feeling disrespected in that moment might sound ridiculous. But that’s the point. A man wants to feel respected by his wife and children he provides for.

Reaching FIRE doesn’t eliminate the desire for respect. It just shrinks the circle of people whose respect you care about. The flip side is that when you don’t get respect from the few people who matter most, it stings far more than any stranger’s opinion ever could.

It’s worth doing an honest self-assessment of your spending on material things.

Maybe you genuinely love watches, cars, clothes, shoes, jewelry, or handbags. That’s fine, as long as you can comfortably pay cash and never carry a revolving credit card balance.

But if you’re buying expensive things you don’t even use or love, you may still be chasing status to earn respect.

Recent findings suggest that maybe the midlife sports car is compensating for something. Maybe the designer wardrobe is a response to someone who once made an unkind comment about your body. Or maybe the nonstop social media highlight reel is an attempt to prove the middle school bullies wrong.

It has been revealed that whatever the reason, it’s worth exploring. Because the people you’re trying to impress are probably too busy trying to impress someone else. Know that there is an incredible joy of being a nobody so long as you have your finances in order.

In a recent development, for many of us in the FIRE community, the desire for stuff fades over time because the need for outside respect fades too. Once you’re living the life you want and own the things you need, strangers have nothing left to grant you. Nobody can hand you a better life than the one you’ve already built.

That’s the real luxury of stealth wealth. Not hiding your money, but no longer needing an audience for it.

Readers, did you go through a loud wealth phase when you were younger? What was your version of the Armani jeans? Do you think materialism is really about respect, or is something else going on? And now that you’re older, whose respect do you still care about, and how do you feel when you don’t get it?

Stealth wealth means nobody else needs to know your net worth. But you should.

People spend thousands on designer clothes to impress strangers. A free expert review of your finances is a far better flex, even if nobody sees it.

Ads & Influencers Still Sell When Labeled – See Fewer of Them

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A “sponsored” label marks an influencer’s post as an ad, but it doesn’t stop the ad from working, so cut how many ads reach you.
  • One home-decor pin leads to a lamp, the lamp to a matching rug and throw pillows, and soon $200 of pieces you didn’t want a week ago is sitting in your cart.
  • Recent findings suggest that ads use the same few tactics again and again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A “sponsored” label marks an influencer’s post as an ad, but it doesn’t stop the ad from working, so cut how many ads reach you. Unfollow or mute shopping accounts, switch off the ad settings that use your browsing elsewhere, and put anything you first saw in a feed on a wish list for a day.

One home-decor pin leads to a lamp, the lamp to a matching rug and throw pillows, and soon $200 of pieces you didn’t want a week ago is sitting in your cart.

Recent findings suggest that ads use the same few tactics again and again. A crossed-out “was” price makes the real price look like a deal. A “limited drop” or a sale that ends Sunday pushes you to buy now. Star ratings and a creator using the product at home suggest everyone loves it. And the fifth time the same lamp demonstrates up in your feed, it feels familiar, which is easy to mistake for wanting it.

Industry observers note that on social apps, those tactics come from creators you follow and from ads that look like your friends’ posts. The FTC revised its Endorsement Guides in 2023. Its guide for influencers tells creators who are paid or given free products to say so in plain words like “ad” or “sponsored,” placed where they’re hard to miss. That label tells you it’s an ad, but it doesn’t stop the tactics from working. The lamp still looks good in a living room you admire, and the fifth sighting still feels familiar.

It has been revealed that so the cheapest defense is seeing fewer ads and sponsored posts. Unfollow or mute the shopping accounts and the creators whose posts mostly sell something. On Instagram, muting hides someone’s posts without unfollowing them, and they aren’t told. Then switch off the ad settings that use your browsing on other sites:.

You’ll still see ads, but they won’t be based on what you browsed on store sites.

Last, put anything you first saw in a feed on a wish list, and give it the full day the 24-hour rule calls for.

After the wait, buy only what you’d have gone looking for without a post showing it to you.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Adventurer to Climb 100 Peaks on 2,000Km Taiwan Traverse

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan.
  • In a recent development, taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character.
  • Recent findings suggest that yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tomorrow, November 1, Japanese adventurer Yoki Tanaka begins a four-month, 2,000km trek north to south down the length of Taiwan. Along the way, he will summit all 100 of Taiwan’s celebrated Baiyue peaks.

In a recent development, taiwan has about 268 peaks exceeding 3,000m, but only 100 of them made this special list, which is based not only on height but beauty, difficulty, prominence, and character. Prominent Taiwanese mountaineers compiled the list in the early 1970s, partly inspired by Japan’s own list of 100 revered mountains.

Recent findings suggest that yoki Tanaka arrives in Taiwan earlier this week. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Industry observers note that the 43-year-old Tanaka has specialized in this unusual combination of long-distance trekking and mountaineering. In 2014, he summited Japan’s 100 famous mountains while walking 7,800km over 208 days. (Japan, though far bigger than Taiwan, has only 23 mountains over 3,000m.) A year later, he extended that by climbing 200 mountains and walking 8,000km in 222 days. Finally, he increased that again to 300 mountains. This time, it took him three years and about 20,000km of walking.

Tanaka’s projected route across Taiwan.

Tanaka will begin on Sunday from the northernmost tip of Taiwan, at the Cape Fugui lighthouse, and finish sometime in March at Eluanbi, the country’s southernmost point. The first 150km will be along roads before he reaches his first trailhead. He’ll spend the next week trekking. His first five peaks will be Xueshan (3,886m), Nanhudashan (3,742m), Hehuanshan (3,417m), Qilaishan (3,560m), and Nenggaoshan 3,262m).

Although he won’t use motorized transport for the entire journey, he will have ample opportunity to resupply along the way. His expedition strategy includes a charmingly precise breakdown of how he intends to spend his evenings: town stays, 48 days; mountain huts, 38 days; tent camping, 39 days. He has also budgeted 16 rest days and 20 contingency days.

According to recent reports, tanaka trains in Taiwan earlier this year. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

His most difficult section, scheduled for early January, will take him through the remote interior of the Central Mountain Range for over two weeks. During this time, he’ll have to carry his own food, search for trails that may no longer exist, and gamble that he will be able to find enough water.

During a December 2025 reconnaissance trip to Xueshan, Taiwan’s second-highest mountain, Tanaka discovered how difficult it can be to obtain water. Two water sources marked on his map were completely dry.

On a previous hike. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

By late January, the Japanese trekker should reach the historic Batongguan Trail, eventually leading to 3,952m Yushan, Taiwan’s highest mountain. The Batongguan Trail was originally constructed in 1875 under the Qing dynasty to establish a route across the mountainous interior. Decades later, Japanese colonial authorities constructed a separate crossing through the region. Sections of the route survive as remote hiking trails and provide access to some of Taiwan’s highest mountains.

Sources indicate that tanaka first visited Taiwan in the spring of 2025 and has made several reconnaissance visits since, including an east-west crossing of the island earlier this year. He had intended to begin his Taiwan 100 Peaks Traverse project this past spring, but local mountaineers advised him to avoid the rainy season and typhoon risks. Their advice prompted him to shift his starting date to November.

Yoki Tanaka on a training hike in Taiwan. Photo: Yoki Tanaka/Instagram.

Industry observers note that interestingly, of Taiwan’s 100 Baiyue peaks, only 99 are now recognized as surpassing 3,000m. The exception is Lushan at 2,981m. It was originally measured at 3,043m but subsequent measurements reduced its elevation. Nevertheless, it remains on the list.

Taiwan’s representative in Japan told Japanese media that the fastest prior completion of the Baiyue by a foreign climber took three years and eight months, spread over multiple trips.

Once Tanaka begins, his expedition website will provide live tracking of his progress across Taiwan.

#102440. Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1846 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Everest 1971: Ambition, Death, and Dispute

📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest.
  • It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort.
  • Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the spring of 1971, only one party attempted to climb Everest. Led by Norman Dyhrenfurth and Jimmy Roberts, this ambitious expedition planned to split into two groups. One party would go for the steep Southwest Face, while the other would attempt the West Ridge.

It was meant to be as much a test of international cooperation as an extraordinary climbing effort. But what happened turned out to be more complicated and controversial than anyone had expected.

Before the team even arrived in Nepal, the venture was heavily commercialized and advertised to the public. The BBC secured exclusive television rights and embedded a nine-person film crew directly into the expedition. At the same time, the British newspaper rights were sold to The Sunday Times, which sent along prominent journalists like Murray Sayle. The media machinery relentlessly hyped the expedition beforehand, boldly framing the climb as a mere formality and setting public expectations for a historic success.

The expedition itself came from a merger of two intends. A British-Norwegian group asked Roberts to lead a Southwest Face attempt. Dyhrenfurth was already organizing the same route, so they joined forces. As the combined team was large, they decided to try two routes at once.

The Southwest Face was the main goal, specifically aiming for a direct, vertical line (a direttissima), while the other group targeted the complete, aesthetic West Ridge route. Both goals were very difficult, and climbers chose their preferred route.

Jimmy Roberts in Nepal. Photo: The Nepal Times.

Sources indicate that the Southwest Face team included British climbers Dougal Haston and Don Whillans, Japanese climbers Naomi Uemura and Reizo Ito, and others. The West Ridge team included Austrian Wolfgang Axt, Swiss climbers Michel and Yvette Vaucher, Norwegian climbers Odd Eliassen and Jon Teigland, American David Isles, and Indian Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna. Frenchman Pierre Mazeaud and Italian Carlo Mauri later joined the West Ridge side.

In total, the whole expedition had 31 foreign climbers from a dozen countries, as well as several Sherpas, including Ang Phurba and Sonam Girme. According to early planning notes, neither leader had personal summit ambitions. Both described themselves as the older men of the team.

The Southwest Face of Everest. Photo: Wikimedia.

Base Camp was established on March 22, 1971, at 5,425m. Both teams worked through the Khumbu Icefall. Dyhrenfurth later noted it was in the most difficult and dangerous state he had ever seen it. They set up Advance Base Camp on the Western Cwm, then separated.

Industry observers note that the Southwest Face team pushed higher. The West Ridge team, with Axt as coordinator, began setting up their own camps, although supplies arrived slowly. Some of the West Ridge climbers didn’t want to carry heavy loads. A long storm in late April made conditions worse for both teams and delayed everything by two to three weeks. Dyhrenfurth’s own account in the American Alpine Journal confirms the early harmony among the team and the exceptional difficulties of the Icefall that spring.

In a recent development, the 1971 Everest expedition. Photo: ‘Surrender to Everest’/imdb.com.

On April 18, Bahuguna and Axt of the West Ridge team were descending from a high camp in a storm at about 7,000m. They were not tied to each other. Axt had left his harness and climbing rope higher up to save weight, knowing fixed ropes were already in place. He crossed a long fixed-rope traverse by hand, waited for Bahuguna, saw him wave, then continued down because he was exhausted. He later heard screams and raised the alarm.

It has been revealed that A rescue party reached Bahuguna still clipped to the fixed rope, about 25m from easier ground. He had lost a mitten and a crampon, and his face was covered by ice. Attempts to lower him failed in the storm and darkness, and he finally died of cold and exhaustion. Bahuguna’s fingers and face were crusted with ice, his eyes were wide, and he could not recognize Whillans or speak.

Major Harsh Vardhan Bahuguna on the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

According to recent reports, according to Roberts’ report in the Himalayan Database, the rescuers had to leave Bahuguna because it would be completely dark in 10 minutes, and the others would freeze too. Roberts later described the death as the result of a series of mistakes by Bahuguna and Axt themselves, and noted that allowing them to go so high alone had been a factor.

Bahuguna’s body was later recovered and cremated near Base Camp.

Industry observers note that dyhrenfurth held an inquiry after the fatal incident. Axt mentioned that the fixed ropes made roping up unnecessary and that he didn’t realize how serious things were until the screams. He later explained that if he had stayed longer, he risked losing his own fingers and toes.

“What should I do? One hour later and I am frozen,” he said. He added that he couldn’t pull Bahuguna himself and had to go down for fresh men.

Sources indicate that mazeaud called it murder through negligence. Dyhrenfurth agreed that Axt should have gone back to look, but said that it was easy to judge after the event. Roberts noted that Bahuguna’s death was very sad but didn’t determine the expedition’s final outcome.

Norman Dyhrenfurth, Carlo Mauri, Yvette Vaucher, Reizo Ito, Pierre Mazeaud, and Michale Vaucher in ‘Surrender to Everest’ (1971). Photo: imdb.com.

In a recent development, after the death and the storm, most of the remaining West Ridge climbers (especially Mazeaud, Mauri and the Vauchers) wanted to abandon both hard routes and switch to the normal South Col route. They stated that it was more practical and gave a better chance of reaching the summit.

Many others, including most of the Southwest Face group and the leading Sherpas, believed that those climbers mainly wanted personal success: first Frenchman, first Italian, or first woman. A vote that included the Sherpas went strongly in favor of putting all remaining effort into the Southwest Face. The West Ridge group noted the decision was a plot to keep them off the summit, so the press would stay focused on the Southwest Face.

Camp 2. Pumori on the left, with snow-and-ice slopes leading to the West Ridge. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

It has been revealed that mazeaud’s radio message remarked that they expected him — a French member of parliament — to work like a Sherpa for Anglo-Saxons and Japanese. He said France had been insulted. Yvette Vaucher called the decision monstrous and said she had lost Everest and her friends at the same time.

According to one account, Roberts told Mazeaud to leave during a loud argument. The four went home in early May, ending further work on the West Ridge. Isles and Teigland later stated that the decision to cancel the West Ridge climb, made in a highly emotional moment after Bahuguna’s death, was a great mistake. Teigland said he had dreamed of the West Ridge for two years.

A virus, diagnosed by some as mononucleosis, spread through the camps and forced many climbers down, including Dyhrenfurth. Bad weather continued to block supplies. With the West Ridge group gone and fewer people left, Haston and Whillans kept pushing on the Southwest Face. Japanese climbers and Sherpas carried heavy loads high on the mountain. Camps were placed up to approx. 8,290m.

Haston and Whillans fixed ropes partway into a chimney in the Rock Band but ran out of rope, oxygen, and food. According to Roberts, they placed Camp 6 at 8,290m and were making progress every day. He remarked they could have traversed onto the South Buttress and reached the summit that way in one day, but that was not the route they had come to climb. Extreme cold hampered them. They needed another camp higher up. They turned back 450m short of the summit on May 21.

In a recent development, roberts later stated weather was the basic cause of failure: Once it goes bad, it affects everything else. He described the expedition as 50 percent successful. They failed to summit, but those who stayed worked well together.

Roberts said that he was bitterly disappointed after three years of work, but apart from Bahuguna’s death, he had nothing to regret. He criticized Schloemmer for contributing almost nothing and said that Axt was asked to come up and help on the Southwest Face but thought it over and went down instead.

It has been revealed that haston called claims that the Austrians were ready to help “complete balls.” He mentioned that when they asked for support at Camp 5, Schloemmer replied that he needed a Sherpa to carry his personal gear. Haston added that he and Whillans were the only ones who could push hard enough to get the route going, and that the Japanese were the only others with real high-Himalayan experience.

Uemura noted that he and Ito helped by carrying loads because that was their obligation, and that if the weather had been good, the expedition could have succeeded. After the 1971 expedition, Uemura decided to always climb solo thereafter.

In a recent development, axt and Schloemmer complained there was no real authority above Advance Base Camp. Axt stated the two British stayed high for three weeks and monopolized the lead, and that without a coordinator to rotate people, there was no room for others. He said if there had been good organization on the Face, he could have succeeded. Isles and Teigland said the international aspect had nothing to do with the failure.

Recent findings suggest that the problems came from personalities and the emotional decision after the death. Mazeaud and the Vauchers maintained that the leaders had broken the original strategy of two routes and prevented them from reaching the summit for publicity reasons. Dyhrenfurth stated the experiment in international climbing was only partially successful, but cooperation had been good until the argument over the route. He noted that the United Nations had tried international cooperation for a long time and had not done too well, either.

In their interesting and detailed post-climb article titled Post-Mortem of an International Expedition for Mountain magazine (later reprinted by The Himalayan Club), authors Ken Wilson and Mike Pearson traced exactly how the initial merger and massive team size doomed the expedition from the start. They concluded that the 1971 expedition’s collapse was primarily driven by severe natural forces, specifically adverse weather and illness, rather than interpersonal friction. They also attributed systemic blame to organizers for combining distinct climbing factions into an unmanageable, oversized team.

Sources indicate that memorial at Everest in 1971 for Harsh Bahuguna. Photo: Wolfgang Axt/The Himalayan Journal.

The questions remain: Was Bahuguna’s death mainly the result of mistakes by the two men involved, or something the leaders should have prevented? Did the decision to drop the West Ridge and focus on the Southwest Face save the expedition or destroy it? And was the international idea itself the problem, or simply the mix of strong personalities, bad weather, and the pressure of being on Everest?

#102439. Tech Report: Will the AI Bubble Destroy our Retirement?
