The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.
  • Sources indicate that I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares.
  • It has been revealed that but naively, I indicated a true order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.

Sources indicate that I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares. That’s 4.6% of my indication, or about $5,000 out of $107,900. I entered my order the morning the books opened, hoping that would signal I was a serious buyer.

It has been revealed that but naively, I indicated a true order. I wanted up to $107,900 of stock to reach my goal of roughly $500,000 in Anthropic exposure through traditional VC, public VC, and direct ownership.

Industry observers note that the embarrassing part is that I should have known better. During my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse, I worked on over 100 IPOs. I went on roadshows, introduced management to my institutional clients, and read demand back to the syndicate desk. Everybody padded their orders. A fund that wanted 500,000 shares would put in for 2 million because it knew the syndicate desk would cut it back.

The problem with being honorable is that you lose when everybody else is inflating their order to get their true allocation. I thought being a Fidelity customer for over 25 years, with my kids’ 529 aims, custodial accounts, Roth IRAs, a SEP IRA, and Solo 401(k)s, would count for something. It clearly didn’t. To them, I’m just a number, like most people who work are.

In a recent development, the allocation process reminded me that if you want to compete in this hyper-competitive world, you have to work the system to your advantage. If you don’t, you will likely lose to those who do.

Sources indicate that to protest my insultingly low allocation, I decided to take the day off. But that’s what I do every day anyway.

Here are some real-life examples where playing fair cost money, time, and happiness.

When my wife and I applied to preschools for our son, we decided not to ask our network to write letters of recommendation to the school heads. Despite having friends who were massive donors and board members, I wanted to see if we could get in on our own merits as a high school tennis coach and his editor wife.

Sources indicate that we could not. Six preschools rejected us after happily taking our $75 to $100 application fees. We only got into our neighborhood preschool through serendipity. We kept running into one of their teachers on paternity leave in Golden Gate Park.

If we had leaned on our connections, we would have saved hundreds in application fees, dozens of hours, and a lot of stress.

It has been revealed that the families who got in weren’t less honorable. They were more effective. Our honor tax came to six rejection letters and several hundred dollars in application fees.

I first thought about starting Financial Samurai in 2006, the year I graduated from Cal’s MBA program. But I didn’t because I felt I needed at least 10 years of finance experience before I had the credibility to write publicly.

It has been revealed that so I waited until the world was falling apart in 2009, 10 years after graduating from William & Mary. The three-year delay cost me revenue, likely earlier book deals, a bigger reputation, and probably pushed back my exit from finance by at least a year. I wrote more about this in Don’t Let Honor And Pride Keep You On Hard Mode Forever.

The internet has shown me time and again that you do NOT need expertise in what you’re talking about or selling. A not-rich 26-year-old can write a book on how to get rich. Someone whose marriage is falling apart and doesn't have kids can host a podcast for couples with kids. Someone with a $100,000 portfolio can become an investing guru on social media.

Plenty of people overlook your experience or credentials. So you might as well put yourself out there and start.

In a recent development, after 13 years of grade school and four years of college, you might have too much pride to accept money from your parents. Making it on your own feels like the honorable thing to do. It’s also good for your self-esteem.

In a recent development, so you sleep on a friend’s couch and lose weight because you can barely afford groceries. Meanwhile, your college friends rent nice two-bedrooms in the city and go out every weekend because their parents are paying. Some even buy their first homes and have their girlfriends move in, courtesy of the Bank of Mom and Dad.

You, on the other hand, turn down an amazing job offer in Fresh York City because it’s way too expensive. Instead, you stay in Des Moines, Iowa, take a $60,000 job with benefits, and feel like you’ve made it.

At your 10-year college reunion, you’ve finally saved $100,000 and are ready to settle down. But the girl you liked moved to NYC to be with your college buddy, who is now a director at a hedge fund making $1 million a year.

He’s worth $7 million and no longer needs his parents’ help. So he buys a $6 million, three-bedroom condo on the Upper West Side, marries your dream girl, and starts a family.

In a recent development, his parents’ help wasn’t a handout. It was a launch pad. Your pride was an anchor. More parents would rather help their adult children while still alive than after they are gone. Accept help with grace.

Sources indicate that in 2012, I wanted out of banking. The classic move would have been to give two weeks’ notice, thank everyone, and walk away. That’s what most people do, leaving their deferred compensation and any chance of severance on the table.

Instead, I negotiated. I offered to train my junior colleague to take over my business, which gave management a smooth transition. In exchange, I kept five years of deferred compensation and walked away with a six-figure severance check. That money gave me a multi-year runway to grow Financial Samurai and remain free.

Had I just quit, my honor tax would have been five years of deferred compensation plus a six-figure severance check. That’s an expensive way to feel good about yourself, when companies treat you as a number and swiftly move on once you’re gone.

I break down the exact process in How To Engineer Your Layoff if you're looking to leave with a severance package as well.

You’d have to be naive to think a wealthy parent who virtue signals about how amazing public schools are, but sends their own kids to private school, would ever give up their kid’s college spot for yours.

The world is extremely cutthroat. Yes, you will have good friends and good people who try to help you. But in most competitive situations, you’re up against people who care about themselves and their families first.

In my IPO example, my competitors were the thousands of other retail investors who wanted shares. If I had inflated my order by 10X, I might have gotten about $50,000 of stock instead of $5,000. With a 15% first-day pop, that’s a $7,500 gain instead of $750.

Recent findings suggest that so whatever credentials or goodwill you have, don’t assume they mean much. At every competitive juncture, you must speak up and market yourself. People will forget who you are and what you’ve done for them if you don’t remind them.

Industry observers note that working the system doesn’t mean lying, cheating, or stepping on people. It means understanding how the game is actually scored so you stop paying an honor tax you don’t owe. Here’s how.

1) Inventory your unfair advantages. Write down your network, capital, credentials, platform, free time, and family support. Most people underestimate what they have because they’ve never made the list.

Industry observers note that 2) Learn how the game is really scored. IPO books get padded. Admissions offices respond to relationships and donations. Many jobs get filled through referrals before they’re ever posted. Find an insider and ask how decisions actually get made. The official rules are often only half the story.

3) Make the ask early. A referral, an introduction, or a note from a board member costs your friend five minutes. Getting rejected six times costs you far more. Most people are happy to help. They just need to be asked.

4) Negotiate everything with leverage. A competing job offer, a severance package, a retention offer from your cable tech giant, a lower rate from your lender. If you don’t ask, the answer is always no.

Industry observers note that 5) Accept help with gratitude, then pay it forward. Taking help from parents, mentors, or friends isn’t weakness. It’s compounding. The honorable part is what you do with the head start.

6) Remind people of your value. Send the enhancement email. Check in with the fund manager. Tell your longtime broker you’d like a bigger allocation next time. Silence gets read as indifference.

Sources indicate that 7) Know your line and your risk. Padding an IPO order is common, but there’s a catch. If demand comes in weaker than expected, you could get filled on everything you asked for. Never inflate an order you can’t afford to pay for. Game the system, but don’t break the law or your word.

According to recent reports, be honorable with your family, your friends, and anyone who trusts you. Keep your word. Pay your debts.

According to recent reports, but when you’re competing for a scarce resource against strangers, following an honor code nobody else follows isn’t noble. It’s expensive. And the cost compounds over decades in the form of lost money, lost time, and lost happiness.

Industry observers note that if you’re a parent, it’s your responsibility to fight to give your children every chance to survive and thrive. Your kids won’t care that you were too proud to make a phone call. They’ll care whether they got the opportunity.

As I wrap up this post, I have a confession. Maybe honor wasn’t the only reason I placed a true order.

Between my traditional venture funds and public venture funds, I already own a meaningful amount of Anthropic. So deep down, I probably felt my exposure was big enough. If I had really needed those shares, I suspect I would have padded my order like everybody else.

It has been revealed that in other words, maybe I just didn’t care that much if my order got cut by 95%. I’m at a stage in life where I should have enough. Missing out on a $7,500 first-day pop won’t change how I live, where my kids go to school, or what time I wake up tomorrow.

According to recent reports, which makes me wonder whether our actions show our real financial position better than our words do. The person who fights hardest for every share, every school spot, and every introduction is often the person who feels they don’t have enough yet. They say they are financially independent, yet stay for one more year at a job they hate. The person who shrugs may simply be full.

So before you judge yourself for being too honorable, or someone else for working the system, ask what each of you actually needs.

Sources indicate that sometimes the honor tax is a choice. Sometimes it’s just a sign you can afford to pay it.

It has been revealed that have you ever lost out because you played by the rules while others didn’t? Did you pad your order in the Anthropic IPO, and how much did you get relative to your true demand? Where do you draw the line between leveraging your advantages and gaming the system unfairly?

Would you accept financial help from your parents to get ahead, or is making it on your own still worth the price? And if you have kids, how hard are you willing to work your network to give them a better shot?

Do you think your willingness to play hardball shrinks once you feel you have enough?

It has been revealed that most people don’t fall behind financially because they’re lazy. They fall behind because they play by rules nobody else follows. They accept the first offer, wait their turn, and hope someone notices.

In Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller, I show you how to build wealth on purpose. It covers the right net worth targets for your age, how to multiply your income, and how to use every advantage you have to reach seven figures and beyond.

In a recent development, building wealth also means getting the big decisions right. Buy This Not That, a WSJ bestseller, is my framework for life’s most expensive choices: how much house to buy, how to invest, how to negotiate, and when to take a risk. One good decision can easily make up for years of honor tax.

  • Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

It has been revealed that the three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

Recent findings suggest that the icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

Industry observers note that the icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

Sources indicate that at the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

Recent findings suggest that the skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

In a recent development, “We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

It has been revealed that inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation.
  • In a recent development, post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way.
  • If you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation. Yes, food costs more. Yes, tuition and health insurance went up again. But our stocks, our homes, and our private investments rose even faster. We felt richer, so we shrugged.

In a recent development, post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way. Real estate is usually the last domino to fall. We are living in the worst-case scenario for anyone building or preserving wealth: higher prices and lower asset values at the same time.

If you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone. My public equity portfolio is overweight tech, and it's taking a beating. I'm down around 20% from the highs, or more than three years of living expenses, and it hurts.

The only silver lining is that FIRE and debt don't mix, which has prevented me from going on margin and losing even more.

Say a household has $1 million in investments and spends $120,000 a year. With 3.7% inflation, its cost of living rises by about $4,400 a year.

It has been revealed that when that portfolio was up 20%, the household gained $200,000. That's 45 years' worth of extra inflation costs. Nobody complains about $4,400 when they're up $200,000.

Industry observers note that now the portfolio is down 12%. That's a $120,000 loss, and the extra $4,400 a year in living costs hasn't gone anywhere. The household didn't just lose its cushion. It's paying more to live while owning less.

Sources indicate that that's why the mood flipped so fast. The wealth effect works in reverse, and it works faster on the way down. Let's look at how we got here, where stocks could go, and how to survive until the bargain gets restored.

After Democrats won both the House and the Senate in the midterms, investors began pricing in a slower AI data-center buildout. The market began to correct.

According to recent reports, then Nvidia, due to the Jensen Huang debacle, and the rest of the AI complex kept sliding. The QQQ just finished its 9th-worst week since its 1999 launch, down 10.5%. That's the worst week since March 2020.

It has been revealed that the S&P 500 closed at 6,910 on Nov 20, about 11.6% below its Oct 6 closing high of 7,819. Another ~9.5% decline to roughly 6,255 and we're officially in a bear market.

Whether you cheered or groaned on election night is irrelevant to your portfolio. The market reprices to future expectations.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, inflation refuses to cooperate. The last annual CPI reading was 3.7% in September. October prices rose 0.4% month-over-month, hotter than expected. Gasoline is up about 37% from a year ago. And the market is pricing in a Fed rate hike in December.

A Fed hiking into a falling stock market is not what the doctor ordered. But it is what we've got.

Here's what makes this downturn different from 2000 or 2008. Corporate earnings are still projected to grow at a healthy clip. Goldman Sachs forecasts S&P 500 earnings of $375 for 2026, $415 for 2027, and $460 for 2028.

Industry observers note that when stocks fall while earnings rise, the only thing that's breaking is the multiple investors are willing to pay. The S&P 500's forward P/E has collapsed from roughly 23x a year ago to 16.5x today. That's a ~29% de-rating in about 13 months. We're also lower than we were during Liberation Day in April 2025.

Industry observers note that in other words, the market isn't saying companies are making less money. It's saying it no longer trusts how fast AI profits will grow, and it wants a bigger margin of safety for the risk.

Sources indicate that here's one of several rosy forecasts by Wall Street firms for year-end 2026 and 2027. I hope it comes true so that my wife and I can keep our FIRE membership card.

At 6,910 and 16.5x, the implied forward earnings are about $418, which lines up neatly with Goldman's $415 estimate for 2027. So let's run the math using $418 in forward earnings.

The first takeaway is counterintuitive. At 16.5x, the S&P 500 is already cheaper than its 5-year and 10-year averages. If valuations simply mean revert to the past decade, the index has 16-20% of upside.

The bear case indicates the last decade was the anomaly. Go back to 1990 on the Goldman chart and the aggregate index spent most of the 2003-2015 period between 13x and 17x. Revert to ~15x and the S&P falls another 7-8%. Revert to the 12.8x lows of the post-financial crisis era and we're looking at another ~23% drop.

It has been revealed that but the bigger risk isn't the multiple. It's the earnings. Here's what happens if AI spending gets throttled and forward earnings fall 10% to ~$376, essentially flat versus 2026.

It has been revealed that the nightmare scenario requires both lower earnings and a lower multiple. That combination gets you to 5,600-5,700, or roughly 28% off the peak. Painful, but in line with a garden-variety bear market, not a 2000-style wipeout.

It has been revealed that my base case is that we're closer to the bottom than the top on valuation, but earnings revisions over the next two quarters will decide whether this is a correction or a bear market. Watch the earnings estimates, not the headlines.

When stock prices fall, CEOs get nervous and CFOs get busy. The easiest way to defend earnings per share is to cut the biggest expense line: people.

The layoffs were already happening before the selloff. Through October, tech companies announced 171,501 job cuts, 21% more than the same period a year earlier, and AI has been the top stated reason for cuts this year. Now add a 10%+ market correction and a Fed that's raising rates. I'm certain more mass layoffs are coming in Q1, after the bonuses are paid.

It has been revealed that I lived through roughly 20 rounds of layoffs during my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse. The people who got cut first were rarely the least talented. They were the least liked, the least visible, and the most expensive relative to their output.

So please be on your best behavior if you want to keep your job. Get in first, leave last, volunteer your time, and support your boss's charitable causes. It's corporate theater, but theater keeps the paychecks coming.

If you don't want to deal with corporate BS anymore, start planning to negotiate a severance package now. The people who get laid off first tend to get the best severance packages. They also get a head start on the hundreds, if not thousands, of employees who will be looking for jobs later.

That's what I did in 2012. Instead of quitting, I negotiated my way out with a severance check that helped fund my first years of early retirement. I lay out the whole playbook in How To Engineer Your Layoff. Leaving a job you no longer like with a severance package feels incredible.

Most downturn advice assumes inflation is falling and the Fed is riding to the rescue with rate cuts. Not this time. When prices go up and asset values go down, you have to defend on four fronts at once.

In a bull market, your portfolio can earn more than your salary. In this environment, your paycheck is the only asset that isn't getting marked down every day. Your job is now your most valuable asset, so treat it that way.

It has been revealed that be the person who uses AI to do the work of two people, not the person AI replaces. Build goodwill with your manager and colleagues before the layoff list gets made. And if you were thinking about quitting, don't. Stick around, collect your paychecks, and see if you can negotiate a severance when cuts inevitably hit your group.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have a second income stream yet, start one now. It doesn't need to replace your salary. It just needs to cover your groceries, which feel like they cost a lot more than they used to. The key to financial freedom is generating enough passive income to cover your basic living expenses.

Industry observers note that if you locked in a low fixed-rate mortgage, congratulations. Inflation is quietly shrinking your debt in real terms. This is not the time to aggressively pay it down and give up liquidity.

With the Fed hiking, cash in a money market fund or Treasury bills finally pays you to wait. Earning over 5% risk-free in US Treasury bonds is a beautiful, beautiful thing.

It has been revealed that favor assets that can reprice with inflation. Rents and replacement costs tend to rise with prices, which is one reason I've always kept a large chunk of my net worth in real estate. Meanwhile, attack the variable expenses that are inflating fastest: gas, food, insurance, and subscriptions you forgot you had.

According to recent reports, personally, I'm eating less due to rising food costs, which is great for my dad bod challenge. I'm also just fixing my car instead of buying a new one. Finally, I've cut many superfluous items such as cable from our budget.

Instead of guessing the bottom, tie your purchases to the forward P/E. At ~$418 in forward earnings, 16x is about 6,690 on the S&P 500, 15x is about 6,270, and 14x is about 5,850. If we get down to these levels, buy a slug at each level and let the market come to you.

Before you buy anything, run a Financial SEER check. It's a way to quantify your risk tolerance, calculating potential loss in terms of time.

For example, if you have $500,000 in stocks and save $5,000 a month, another 20% drop costs you $100,000, or 20 months of work. If that makes you sick, you're already too aggressive, and buying more won't help you sleep.

According to recent reports, above all, avoid selling your best assets to fund a lifestyle that inflation made more expensive. That's how a temporary loss becomes a permanent one. Always stay disciplined when there's a chance we're heading into a zombie apocalypse.

It has been revealed that if you're retired, this is a good time to lower your withdrawal rate and ride it out. As I wrote recently, FIRE in a bear market can actually be comforting. When Return On Effort falls, it's the perfect time to work less, not more.

If you have kids, a downturn is a gift. use corrections to help make your kids millionaires. During this selloff, I transferred $23,000 into each of my children's custodial accounts and bought stocks. The more the market fell on Friday, November 20, the more I transferred. And I will continue to transfer cash to their accounts and buy if the market goes lower.

According to recent reports, personally, I've accepted that I can't make money in the stock market right now. Every rally gets sold, and checking my portfolio feels hopeless. So I've stopped trying to fight it. I'm tired of the volatility.

Instead, I'm spending more time with my kids and fixing things around the house. For a couple of years, thick, heavy wallpaper had been peeling off in our downstairs hallway. It looked terrible, so I finally hired professionals to strip it, patch and sand, then prime and paint the walls. Then I spent an hour filling in imperfections and painting as well.

In a recent development, it looks great now. When the market won't reward your effort, put your money and energy into something you can actually see improve. This is why having an internal locus of control feels so good. You're not helpless.

And please keep living your life. The market doesn't care how miserable you are, so you might as well enjoy the holidays with your family.

It's easy to forget during a selloff, but downturns are temporary and time in the market is what builds wealth.

It has been revealed that bear markets transfer wealth from the impatient to the patient. They also reveal who was swimming naked with too much risk, too little cash, and too much confidence in their job security.

You don't need to be a hero. You just need to survive with your job, your cash flow, and your sanity intact. Do that, and the next bull market will take care of the rest.

Readers, are you more worried about losing your job or losing more money in the markets? Where do you think the S&P 500 bottoms if earnings estimates start getting cut? Are you buying the dip in tranches, hoarding cash, or doing nothing at all? And for those who lived through 2000 and 2008 with a significant amount of capital, does this downturn feel different given how strong earnings still are?

That's why I like real estate that benefits from the AI buildout without riding the daily swings of the Nasdaq. I am so sorry to hear of your situation; it's a lot. I've had a friend pass (for whom I was her Executor) and I managed a lot of the details when my FIL passed in 20224. These are the things to take care of now:- Make sure his life insurance clearly notes you as his beneficiary.- Make sure that all bank accounts have joint ownership and clear beneficiary designations.- Make sure his IRAs and 401(k)s have clear beneficiary designations. I've seen prior designations lapse when the HR systems are updated at work, so it's worth checking.- Make sure you have at least 2 credit cards in your name only.- Make sure you have his password manager info, and a list of passwords for important accounts: social media, memberships, etc.- Make sure that you are listed on all utility accounts.- Make sure you have a will, health care proxy, and HIPAA release for him in your records. Also - whatever his Do Not Resuscitate desires are, as well as medical donor information on file.- Make sure any vehicles are titled as His OR Her Name on the title. AAA will help you with title changes as a membership benefit. Totally worth doing, as any physical property not in joint accounts could trigger probate.- Make sure you have copies of all life insurance policies. My FILs was found in a box of old work papers. If we hadn't sorted all of his paper carefully, MIL would have missed out on $60k.- Make sure you have a copy of his birth certificate, and your marriage certificate. You'll need this for any Social Security claims for your son.Sending strength and courage - this is hard work, but you have an opportunity to handle business with some runway, which is a blessing.Statistics: Posted by Sandi_k — Wed Nov 25, 2026 12:38 am.

#102396. Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

Leonard Clark: Explorer, Spy, Liar

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.
  • Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy?
  • A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Born in 1907, Leonard Francis Clark was an explorer, war hero, and writer who made daring expeditions all over the world before dying mysteriously in Venezuela in 1957.

Today, he isn’t well known, but has this lack of scrutiny been a blessing in disguise for this forgotten explorer’s legacy? His books, filled with adventure and excitement, read like fiction. The more one digs into the forgotten reports and old newspaper articles, the stranger his story, and the more complicated the man.

A Tibetan expedition under Leonard Clark in 1949. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Industry observers note that the main sources on Leonard Clark are all, well, Leonard Clark. This isn’t necessarily damning, but it is something he shares with most good con artists or cult leaders. The following is a short biography based only on official records, such as draft cards and census data. The first rule of reading historical accounts is that every historical figure is a liar.

According to recent reports, leonard Francis Clark was born in British Columbia, Canada, in January 1907 to two Americans, Maud and Francis Clark. In 1909, they moved back to Maud’s birth state of California, and Francis promptly died.

According to recent reports, there are conflicting statements online about which university he attended, but census data shows him living only a few kilometers from the University of California (now the University of California, Berkeley) in 1930, so I’d put my money on that one. He began traveling right out of college, spending three years in Borneo on a hunting trip with his brother, Laurence. By the late 1930s, he was on a National Geographic-funded expedition to the South China Sea.

Photo: National Geographic Archives.

Sources indicate that his article, cryptically titled Among the Significant Knot Lois of Hainan, was published in the 1938 September edition. In it, he recounts how he and a small expeditionary force landed in the midst of a deadly cholera epidemic. Relying on hired porters to carry their supplies, Clark and Nicol Smith, another future travel writer, set off into the interior. Soon, malaria and infection laid low most of the team, including, per Clark’s article, Smith.

Again, according to Clark, Smith urged him to take the remaining five porters, the minimum of equipment, and keep going.

Much of the article is dedicated to ethnographic observations, with the typical exoticism and patronizing tone of the era. At one point, Clark noted that the Li people of Hainan reminded him of indigenous Amazonian people and “the men were tall, many six feet.”.

It has been revealed that A recent study demonstrated that the average height for men in Hainan today is 168.7cm, around 5’6″, and the same study found that average heights had increased over the past century. This is a small nitpick, but he’ll repeat this unlikely claim again in the Amazon. It is worth noting that the “six-foot-tall Indian warrior” was a stock character in contemporary pulp adventure fiction.

There is an interesting contrast between Clark’s account and some of the newspaper reports, especially one from a Virginia paper, which relied on Smith for the story. This article implies Smith did much more than lay around his tent with malaria. Clark’s article claims he was the first white man to enter 47 different villages, while the newspaper indicates that Smith was the first Westerner to penetrate inland.

Recent findings suggest that there is a third source: the 37-minute silent film compiled from the expedition’s footage and photographs. In it, we briefly see a white man lying under a mosquito net as if ill. But whether this is Smith, Clark — who admits himself to experiencing malaria symptoms on the expedition — or the third westerner on the expedition, one Jack Munroe, the film doesn’t say.

Photo: National Geographic Archive.

His previous experience in the region led him to return a few years later, this time on behalf of the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS), a precursor to the CIA. His work during the war centered around the China-Burma-India corridor, particularly the Yellow River valley. He was involved in organizing guerrilla activities, building intelligence networks, and navigating the Japanese surrender of Taiwan.

Sources indicate that in a later press statement, Clark explained how he had worked with General Dai Li, and that “the Reds had it in for him,” due to the infamously repressive actions Dai Li took against Chinese Communists. Dai Li, whom historian Barbara Tuchman called “China’s combination of Himmler and J. Edgar Hoover,” was killed in a 1946 plane crash. Wide speculation places the blame for this crash on either the Chinese Communist Party or the OSS. This would make things awkward for Clark a few years later.

He continued his government work in the area after the Second World War, sliding right into the developing Cold War. In 1949, Clark led a large, well-funded expedition into Tibet.

It would have gotten him in the history books if Leonard Clark identified a peak higher than Everest. Unfortunately for him, he didn’t. But he certainly proposed that he had, when he claimed that he’d surveyed Amne Machin and found it to be 9,040m high.

Amne Machin is not taller than Everest. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Clark published his account of the expedition years later, titled The Marching Wind. In it, he wrote with his typical style: daring escapes, stereotypically aggressive natives, and breezy adventure writing. What it did not contain was the data to support his claims.

As soon as he released his first report and measurements, geographers, geologists, and mountaineers pored over them. Bradford Washburn, a cartographer, photographer, and explorer, published a thorough examination of the surveying techniques and questionable results from Clark’s expedition.

Sources indicate that A contemporary review in the Alpine Journal, commenting on his photographic evidence, wrote that “anything more unconvincing could hardly be imagined — yet, ostensibly…the mountain was the object of the expedition.” More on that “ostensibly” later. Suffice it to say, Clark’s estimate that Amne Machin could be almost 1,000m taller than Everest was not adopted by geographers at large.

According to recent reports, the review concluded that “it can hardly be wondered if mountaineers, whom Mr. Clark rather despises, cannot accept his results.”.

Clark blithely remarked that he had “some rather bulky complaints by mountain and other specialists,” but admitted subpar instruments made his results “indecisive.”.

It has been revealed that A surveying party including Clark, far right, taking observations of Amne Machin. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Sources indicate that if he doesn’t seem too broken up, it may be because Amne Machin’s height wasn’t the main purpose of his trip. Clark was supported logistically and went on behalf of Ma Bufang, the fiercely anti-communist warlord ruling Qinghai, on the border of Tibet. Anticipating that he could not long hold out against the People’s Liberation Army, Clark proposed that his expedition would map a path of retreat. This would help Ma Bufang’s army cross into Tibet and continue their anti-Communist campaign from the mountains.

Clark envisioned Ma Bufang’s Qinghai, through Tibet, becoming “the bulwark against Red invasion of India.” Clark went on the expedition and did his mapping, but the PLA took Qinghai only months later, and Ma Bufang fled to Hong Kong.

In his introduction to his book, Clark claims that the United States was unaware of his “very slight aid” to Ma Bufang and local anti-Communist guerrilla activities, and he involved himself with the Chinese Nationalist army “as a private American citizen.” If I were to say that I was skeptical of this claim, I would not be the first to do so. But that falls under speculation, so I will say only that I sent a Freedom of Information Act request to the CIA regarding Clark’s work in Tibet. However, the records were not forthcoming.

After returning from the mountains, Clark went to a wedding anniversary celebration in Canton, surrounded by his fellow Allied intelligence members and their set. Things got a little out of hand, and Clark soon found himself in a Cantonese jail with a bullet wound and two manslaughter charges.

Chinese Nationalist soldiers on Clark’s Tibetan expedition. Photo: The Marching Wind.

Industry observers note that the other two men involved were Harold Harris, an Englishman who died immediately, and Willard Freeman from Massachusetts, who died later from his injuries. Clark also sustained a gunshot wound, but had recovered sufficiently by late November to be moved from hospital to prison.

Recent findings suggest that the three had been drinking together in Freeman’s home when, at about 4 am, servants reported hearing gunshots. Mrs. Maya Freeman entered the room at 10 am to find an odd and grisly scene. Harris, fully clothed, lay dead on Freeman’s bed with three gunshot wounds. Freeman, completely nude, was also lying on the bed, alive with two shots to the abdomen. Clark, in his underwear, was on a second bed, with a single gunshot to the chest. Furniture was overturned, indicating a fight, and all three were covered in scratches. The only weapon found was Clark’s .32 caliber pistol.

Later that month, the Canton District Court denied Clark’s bail request. The court, still trying to determine what exactly happened, focused on the widowed Maya Freeman. Interviewing her for hours, they attempted to make her confess to an affair with Clark. Both of them repeatedly denied it. Clark further denied that he had fired any of the six shots, though he didn’t name the shooter.

In a recent development, clark’s brother contacted former OSS head General William Donovan, who rallied the State Department. Clark reportedly was concerned that if he wasn’t released before the city fell to the Communists, he would be tortured for information regarding Dai Li and OSS activities. The State Department investigated and, thanks to its intervention, Clark was released.

Industry observers note that clark’s legal troubles were splashed across newspapers worldwide. Photo: The Journal (Caldwell, Ohio) November 24, 1949.

According to recent reports, what exactly happened in Freeman’s house that night? Was the dispute between the Allied Intelligence men personal, or professional? If the world were ever to find out, it wouldn’t be from Clark. Once freed, Clark returned to California and moved on to his next adventure. It was an ambitious one: Leonard Clark was going to discover the lost city of El Dorado.

It has been revealed that he had an old parchment map to the lost city, he claimed, which showed it lay in the upper reaches of Peru. Never mind that it had been pretty well established for over a century that El Dorado was a myth, following the efforts of explorers Alexander von Humboldt and Robert Schomburgk.

Clark’s resulting account, The Rivers Ran East, contains all the genre tropes you would expect from a fictional work in the same setting. Native Amazonians are ferocious cannibals who capture Clark and keep him in a poison snake pit, crocodiles can and must be lassoed (there are no crocodiles in Peru, only caimans, a type of alligator), and there is a beautiful lady explorer, Inez Pokorny, who is secretly part of a London-based international El Dorado-seeking organization. If this organization existed, I have found no trace of it outside of this book.

If I were to list every blatant impossibility in his account, we would be here for days, so I’ll just continue on one particular thread: Leonard Clark seems to have a very loose grasp of which animals are in Peru and how significant they are. At one point, he is blinded by a venom-spitting snake. There are three venom-spitting snake species, and none of them are in South America.

His 500-pound (227kg) boars must be peccaries, pig-like animals native to the Americas. The Amazon native white-lipped peccary tops out around 40kg, while the unconfirmed giant peccary still has only been estimated at 50kg. Likewise, his 12m-long pythons must be anacondas, which have a maximum recorded length of eight meters.

Clark claims to have found El Dorado. What he found was a group of Chicham people panning for gold, who traded some of it to Clark and Pokorny. According to his book, Clark traveled under the pretense of investigating botanical medicines, while actually searching for El Dorado.

In fact, as the El Dorado adventures on the page grew more and more ridiculous, I began to wonder if it were not the other way around. Here I have fully entered the realm of speculation. American corporations were, and still are, extremely interested in extracting resources from South America, including pharmaceuticals. In fact, Clark also reported success in this area, claiming to have identified over 60 native medicinals with commercial possibility — as well as Amazonian oil.

In praise of Clark’s work, Baron Wolfenegg, Director of Colonization for the Orient in Peru, accidentally stated the quiet part out loud, stating he’d “learned much from this book that will help my work of colonizing this vast jungle.”.

On Peru’s Perené River. Photo: The Rivers Ran East.

Recent findings suggest that it is practically gauche for explorers to die in their beds, and Clark, who seemed to mold his life to the shape of adventure stories, was no exception. Clark was in Venezuela in 1957, looking, he claimed, for diamond mines. He entered the Amazon basin, never to emerge again.

One history of the OSS offhandedly mentions that Clark died with “two native arrows in his back.” I suspect the explorer’s penchant for sensationalism survived his death. Other contemporary reports describe Clark as having drowned when his canoe overturned.

As I pointed out earlier, most of the information on Clark’s expeditions came from Clark himself. Since he never returned, startlingly little information is available about his death at age 49.

In a recent development, the area around the Orinoco River in Venezuela is, in fact, rich in diamond deposits. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

The line between fact and fiction is notoriously vague in much of the adventure travel genre. Is Herman Melville telling the full truth about his time spent on the island of Nuku Hiva? Did anyone actually complete the “Long Walk” out of a Soviet detention camp, which Slavomir Rawicz falsely claimed as his own tale? How much artistic license and embellishment is acceptable before exploration accounts become outright hoaxes?

Industry observers note that I didn’t write this article with the goal of proving Leonard Clark a charlatan. It can hardly be denied that he really was going to these places, at the very least. But there are enough discrepancies and inaccuracies in his accounts to conclude that they should be taken with a grain of salt, and his treasure-hunting pseudo-archaeological tendencies make his anthropological findings, well, questionable.

As a contemporary New Yorker book critic put it, Clark had “the same gift, or weakness, for grandiose verbiage that got Marco Polo in trouble with his fellow Venetians.”.

The real story, and one which may never be fully disentangled, lies in why, exactly, Clark was doing his exploring. Somewhere between the romantic adventurer and the cynically colonialist spy using exploration as a guise for the extractive, violent enforcement of Western capitalist hegemony, lies the truth.

“Every explorer has two faces,” Clark wrote in the opening to The Rivers Ran East; “the secret one and the one he reveals to the world.”.

#102393. The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1395 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • Sources indicate that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent new route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

Sources indicate that the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman noted. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two newly introduced routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

Bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

It has been revealed that “The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he said.

Sources indicate that he explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

The unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

It has been revealed that “[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

One unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman notes this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

“Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

“Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

It has been revealed that asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

The team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

The base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Sources indicate that the team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

In a recent development, steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

Industry observers note that at the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Industry observers note that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment concerns, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he said.

In the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

It has been revealed that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he noted. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

According to recent reports, heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

The summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that however, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

According to recent reports, route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

Sources indicate that the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to new terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman said.

They then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

According to recent reports, descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Industry observers note that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The latest 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#102391. Tech Report: Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1052 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • Recent findings suggest that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

Recent findings suggest that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an important figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up looks for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

As the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

According to recent reports, though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Industry observers note that some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

The depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

Industry observers note that the main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

In a recent development, attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

Recent findings suggest that the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Industry observers note that despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” says Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

The columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

Sources indicate that according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

There have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

It has been revealed that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Industry observers note that vasiliev said that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Baia notes the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

In a recent development, the Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Recent findings suggest that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

Recent findings suggest that I was going to respond to this post earlier this morning, but the phone rang or something. Anyway…I’m 63, have had a bronze ACA plan with Kaiser SoCal (San Diego) for the past decade. I’m also a (2x now) cancer survivor. First, a rare and aggressive cancer, now something also aggressive but much more common. Just the luck of the draw, I guess. As I’m getting closer to 65, and thinking about what I’m going to do, I think I’m probably going to just stick with Kaiser. I think in these discussions we spend a lot of energy pondering about edge cases. Scary rare diseases that you’re probably not going to get, because, well, they’re rare. My experience is that if the Kaiser doc doesn’t know, they’ll find a colleague who does, even if the colleague is outside of Kaiser. In my case, when things got complicated, they set up a consult for me with Johns Hopkins. Paid for by Kaiser, I assume, because I never saw a bill. I also discovered that is is considerably cheaper to private pay for a consult or two every year at UCSD, than it is to pay for insurance that covers UCSD, and if the world class guy at UCSD makes a recommendation, my Kaiser doc is perfectly capable of executing on it. Honestly, for most life threatening things that you’re likely to come down with, the standard of care is basically a flow chart that everybody follows. When I went to UCSD for the second opinion, even for the rare cancer, the treatment recommendation was exactly the same as what Kaiser offered, and the UCSD doc remarked to stick with Kaiser. He also said that if the cancer became advanced, he might have things to offer, and he could get Kaiser to refer me then. Which fortunately hasn’t happened yet.Statistics: Posted by quantAndHold — Wed Nov 25, 2026 1:58 am.

#102383. Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1282 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing newly introduced route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • Industry observers note that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing newly introduced route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

Industry observers note that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin remarked. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

According to recent reports, this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” noted Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

According to recent reports, for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he said.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

It has been revealed that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson mentioned. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

In a recent development, thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That noted, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

According to recent reports, buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they mentioned. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the big cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

To deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

It has been revealed that ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin mentioned.

“That is why it is important to consider all options and potential challenges before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

According to recent reports, asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

The Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they said. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles said. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he noted.

The climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they stated.
